_note: The two parts of `Core/Crypto` that are pure arithmetic and therefore drift silently if each renderer writes its own: the uniform-integer rejection bound and the UUID bit layouts (parity/F15-crypto.md). `randomBytes % range` is NOT uniform unless range divides 2^32 exactly, and the skew is measurable in any shuffle or raffle built on it; bounds[] pins the largest exact multiple, picks[] pins that a draw at or above it is DISCARDED rather than folded, and distribution[] pins the statistical outcome over a large sample. uuidV7[] pins the RFC 9562 layout byte for byte, which is what makes a v7 id minted on iOS sort against one minted in a browser.

bounds.name: a range of one accepts every draw
a power of two divides exactly, so nothing is ever rejected
a six-sided die rejects the top four draws
a seven-sided range rejects the top four as well
one short of the full space
a range wider than 32 bits is not a range

picks.name: the first draw survives and folds
a draw at the bound is REJECTED, not folded
every draw above the bound is rejected in turn
a single-value range consumes one draw and returns it
negative ranges fold the same way
an inverted range is refused before any draw is taken
a range wider than 32 bits is refused
running out of draws is exhausted, never a biased fallback

distribution._note: The statistical half of DONE WHEN 3. Draw `samples` uniform integers over the inclusive range and assert every bucket lands within `tolerance` (a fraction of the expected count). Wide enough that a correct implementation never flakes, tight enough that a modulo-biased one fails: over 60000 draws of a 0..99 range, modulo bias on a 32-bit draw is far below this bound, so the runner ALSO checks the exact rejection arithmetic in picks[] rather than relying on the sample alone.

uuidV4.name: all-zero entropy still carries the version and variant nibbles
all-ones entropy is masked, not passed through

uuidV7.name: a real timestamp lands in the first 48 bits, big-endian

monotonic._note: The whole reason to prefer v7 for a local id: successive milliseconds produce ids that sort in mint order as plain strings, with maximal entropy in every other bit. If this ever fails, a v7 primary key stops appending to the index and the reason to offer v7 at all is gone.

limits._note: randomBytes is bounded because an unbounded allocation is reachable from markup.
